title: Capacitors and Electrostatic Energy
short_intro: A capacitor is a passive electrical component designed to store electrostatic energy in an electric field established between two conductive plates separated by a dielectric medium. Its capacitive property is quantified by the ratio of the magnitude of charge on either conductor to the potential difference between them.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of capacitance, parallel plate capacitor formula, spherical and cylindrical capacitors, grouping of capacitors in series and parallel, electrostatic energy density.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Dielectrics with polarization vector P, electric displacement vector D, boundary conditions across dielectric interfaces, forces on capacitor plates, transient RC charging and discharging circuits.

prerequisites: Coulomb's Law and Electric Field Intensity

concept_notes.heading: Capacitance of Conductors and Parallel Plate Capacitors
bullets: The capacitance C of a system of two conductors is defined as C = Q / V, where Q is the magnitude of charge on each conductor and V is the potential difference between them.
For a parallel plate capacitor with plate area A and separation d in a vacuum, the capacitance is given by C = epsilon_0 A / d, assuming edge effects are negligible (d << sqrt{A}).
The presence of a uniform dielectric medium of relative permittivity epsilon_r (or dielectric constant K) increases the capacitance to C = K epsilon_0 A / d.

concept_notes.heading: Combination of Capacitors
bullets: In a series combination, identical charge Q resides on each capacitor, and the reciprocal of the equivalent capacitance is the sum of the reciprocals of individual capacitances: 1 / C_s = sum (1 / C_i).
In a parallel combination, the potential difference V across each capacitor is identical, and the equivalent capacitance is the algebraic sum: C_p = sum C_i.

Energy is conserved in parallel charging/discharging processes, but electrostatic energy is generally lost as heat or electromagnetic radiation when connecting uncharged and charged capacitors in parallel.

concept_notes.heading: Electrostatic Energy Storage and Energy Density
bullets: The work done in charging a capacitor to charge Q and potential V is stored as potential energy U = (1/2) Q V = (1/2) C V^2 = (1/2) Q^2 / C.
The electrostatic energy is localized in the electric field between the plates with an energy density u = (1/2) epsilon_0 E^2 for a vacuum.
In a dielectric medium, the energy density becomes u = (1/2) epsilon E^2 = (1/2) K epsilon_0 E^2.

concept_notes.heading: Effect of Dielectrics and Polarization
bullets: When a dielectric is placed in an external electric field E_0, molecular dipoles align, creating an internal polarization field E_p in the opposite direction.
The net electric field within the dielectric is reduced to E = E_0 - E_p = E_0 / K.
The electric displacement vector is defined as D = epsilon_0 E + P = epsilon E, where P is the polarization vector.

derivations.title: Capacitance of a Parallel Plate Capacitor with a Dielectric Slab
derivations.conditions: A dielectric slab of thickness t (t < d) and relative permittivity epsilon_r is inserted between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor of area A and separation d.
steps: The surface charge density on the plates is sigma = Q / A, producing an electric field in the vacuum gap of E_0 = sigma / epsilon_0 = Q / (epsilon_0 A).
Inside the dielectric slab of thickness t, the electric field is reduced to E = E_0 / epsilon_r.
The total potential difference V between the plates is the sum of potentials across the vacuum gap (d - t) and the dielectric slab (t): V = E_0 (d - t) + E t = E_0 [(d - t) + t / epsilon_r].
Substitute E_0 = Q / (epsilon_0 A) into the potential equation: V = \frac{Q}{epsilon_0 A} left[(d - t) + \frac{t}{epsilon_r}\right].
Using C = Q / V, invert the potential expression to find the effective capacitance.

derivations.title: Electrostatic Energy Stored in a Capacitor
derivations.conditions: Charging a capacitor from zero charge to a final charge Q at constant capacitance C.
steps: Suppose at any instant t, the charge on the capacitor is q and the potential difference is v = q / C.
The work done dW in transferring an infinitesimal charge dq from one plate to the other against the existing potential difference is dW = v dq = (q / C) dq.
Integrate the incremental work from q = 0 to the final charge Q to find the total work W: W = int_{0}^{Q} \frac{q}{C} dq.
Evaluating the integral yields W = \frac{1}{C} left[ \frac{q^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{Q} = \frac{Q^2}{2C}.
Using Q = CV, express the stored energy in alternative forms: U = \frac{1}{2} CV^2 = \frac{1}{2} QV.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Charge vs Potential Difference (Q-V Graph)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear straight line passing through the origin on a Q (y-axis) versus V (x-axis) coordinate system.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the Q-V line represents the capacitance C of the capacitor. The area under the Q-V graph represents the total electrostatic potential energy stored in the capacitor.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually for energy calculation and interpretation of linear proportionality between charge and voltage.

graphs_and_experiments.title: RC Circuit Charging Current vs Time Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An exponential decay curve starting from maximum current I_0 = V/R at t = 0 and asymptotically approaching zero as t \to infty.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the transient behavior of current in a series resistor-capacitor network. The time constant \tau = RC determines the rate of decay.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently evaluated in numerical questions involving time constants, voltage growth, and current decay in PGT examinations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Energy Density vs Electric Field Magnitude
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic curve of energy density u on the vertical axis plotted against electric field E on the horizontal axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the quadratic dependence of stored electrostatic energy per unit volume on the local electric field intensity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Useful for analytical problems requiring spatial integration of energy fields in complex geometries.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the equivalent capacitance of three capacitors of values 2 mu F, 3 mu F, and 6 mu F connected in series.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for capacitors in series: 1 / C_s = 1 / C_1 + 1 / C_2 + 1 / C_3.
Find the common denominator (6): 1 / C_s = (3 / 6) + (2 / 6) + (1 / 6) = 6 / 6 = 1 mu F^{-1}.
Invert to find C_s: C_s = 1 mu F.

solved_numericals.question: A parallel plate capacitor has plate area 2 cm^2 and plate separation 2 mm. Calculate its capacitance in vacuum.
solution_steps: Convert units to SI: A = 2 cm^2 = 2 \times 10^{-4} m^2, d = 2 mm = 2 \times 10^{-3} m.
Recall the permittivity of free space: epsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12} F/m.
Apply the parallel plate capacitance formula: C = epsilon_0 A / d.

solved_numericals.question: A parallel plate capacitor of capacitance C is charged to potential V and then isolated. A dielectric slab of dielectric constant K = 4 and thickness equal to half the plate separation is inserted between the plates. Find the new potential difference across the capacitor.
solution_steps: Initial state: Capacitance is C, charge is Q = CV, energy is stored with initial plate separation d.
When a dielectric slab of thickness t = d/2 and K = 4 is inserted, use the capacitance formula with a dielectric slab: C' = \frac{epsilon_0 A}{d - t + (t / K)}.

Substitute t = d/2: C' = \frac{epsilon_0 A}{d - (d/2) + (d / (2 \times 4))} = \frac{epsilon_0 A}{(d/2) + (d/8)} = \frac{epsilon_0 A}{(5d/8)} = \frac{8}{5} left(\frac{epsilon_0 A}{d}\right) = \frac{8}{5} C.
Since the capacitor is isolated, the charge Q remains constant: Q = C V = C' V'.
Calculate the new potential V': V' = (C / C') V = (C / (8/5 C)) V = (5/8) V.

assumptions_and_limitations: Edge effects are neglected in parallel plate capacitor formulas, assuming lateral dimensions are infinitely larger than plate separation (d << sqrt{A}).
Dielectric media are assumed to be linear, isotropic, and homogeneous unless stated otherwise.
Conductors are assumed to be equipotential surfaces with negligible internal resistance during charging transients.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Capacitance depends on the total charge stored on the plates and the applied voltage.
common_misconceptions.correct: Capacitance is purely a geometric property of the conductor arrangement and the intervening medium; it is independent of Q and V.
common_misconceptions.why: The ratio Q/V remains constant because any increase in Q produces a proportional increase in V.

common_misconceptions.wrong: When a battery is disconnected from a capacitor and a dielectric is inserted, the potential difference across the plates remains constant.
common_misconceptions.correct: The charge remains constant when isolated, causing the potential difference to decrease by a factor of K.
common_misconceptions.why: Isolation ensures charge conservation (Q = constant), whereas connection to a battery ensures voltage conservation (V = constant).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Connecting two identical capacitors in parallel doubles the stored energy for the same initial voltage.
common_misconceptions.correct: The total stored energy remains the same if an uncharged capacitor is connected in parallel with an identical pre-charged capacitor to share the charge.
common_misconceptions.why: Half of the initial electrostatic energy is dissipated as heat and spark radiation during the charge redistribution process.

quick_revision: Capacitance C = Q/V depends only on geometry and medium permittivity.
For parallel plates, C = epsilon_0 A / d; inserting a dielectric of constant K increases C by a factor of K.
Energy stored in a capacitor is U = (1/2)CV^2 = Q^2/(2C) = (1/2)QV.
Energy density in an electric field is u = (1/2)epsilon_0 E^2.
In series combinations, charge is invariant; in parallel combinations, potential difference is invariant.
